title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
body:
Summary:
This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning methodology, reliability initiatives, incident review requirements, operational tooling expectations, and runbook templates. It consolidates current practice into a single reference for oncall, engineering, and product teams.

Goals:
- Maintain predictable, measurable reliability for customer-facing inference services (hosted API, dedicated pools, private deployments).
- Ensure a clear, actionable error budget policy tied to remediation and rollout controls.
- Provide a repeatable capacity planning cadence that aligns capacity with forecasted demand and SLOs.
- Standardize incident review and postmortem processes to drive continuous reliability improvements.
- Document required operational tooling and runbooks for major failure modes.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all production services owned by eng-sre and eng-serving-runtime that impact customer-facing inference: api-gateway, inference-router, runtime-pool-manager, kv-cache, model-loader, telemetry-ingest.
- Does not define experimental or pre-prod SLOs (see eng-platform test SLOs doc).

1) SLOs and Error Budgets
Overview:
- Every production service must publish at least one Availability SLO and one Latency SLO (if latency materially impacts customers).
- SLOs are measured on a rolling 28-day window by default. Monthly SLOs are supported for long-lived contracts (e.g., Dedicated).

Required SLO metadata (per service):
- Service name: (e.g., inference-router)
- Owner: (team and primary oncall)
- SLO ID: generated per naming convention slo:<service>:<metric>:<window>
- SLO target: availability (e.g., 99.95% / 28d), latency (e.g., p95 < 250ms), error rate (e.g., < 0.5% 5xx)
- Measurement source: prometheus job, datadog query, or telemetry-aggregate job
- Window: 28d | 7d | 30d
- Burn calculation: exposures (requests) weighted by customer tier if applicable

Example SLOs:
- inference-router.availability.28d = 99.95% (success defined as HTTP 2xx/3xx within 2s)
- runtime-pool-manager.latency.p95.28d = < 500ms (API control-plane operations)

Error budget policy:
- Error budget = 100% - SLO_target. For availability 99.95% -> monthly budget = 0.05% of requests allowed to fail.
- Burn rate thresholds and actions (applies per-window unless overridden by contract):
  1. Green (0-50% consumed): track, no action required.
  2. Yellow (50-75% consumed): service owner notified, reliability initiative backlog reviewed.
  3. Red (75-100% consumed): require a short-term mitigation plan within 24 hours; restrict risky rollouts (no canaries > 10% traffic); schedule immediate RFC if root cause unclear.
  4. Exhausted (>=100% consumed): block major rollouts and require rollback of any recent deploys linked to burn; escalation to SRE lead and product manager; incident review within 72 hours.

SLO Change and Rollout Policy:
- Changes to SLO targets require an ADR and approval from SRE lead + Product.
- If increased risk to customer SLAs is expected, increases to SLO targets must include a rollback plan and compensating reliability initiative.

2) Capacity Planning
Cadence and owners:
- Quarterly capacity planning cycle led by eng-sre capacity_planning working group. Attendance: SRE leads, runtime infra, product ops, sales for large commitments.
- Monthly short-cycle forecast for burst/billing alignment.

Inputs and forecasting model:
- Inputs: historical qps by route, per-request token distribution, average sequence length, model family, customer committed concurrency (Dedicated), seasonality adjustments, planned launches, and marketing campaigns.
- Baseline forecast = SUM_{routes}(expected_qps * avg_tokens * token_cpu_cost_factor) + safety_margin
- Safety margin: default 30% for hosted API, configurable per service (10-50%) depending on SLA and customer commitments.

Scaling thresholds and actions:
- CPU/GPU utilization thresholds (per cluster):
  - Warning: 60% sustained for 1h -> schedule scale-up and prepare autoscaler parameters
  - Critical: 75% sustained for 15m -> trigger autoscale immediate + paging to capacity owners
  - Emergency: 90% sustained for 5m -> admission control, degrade non-critical routes, enable overflow to Dedicated pool if configured
- Queue backpressure: request-queue-latency p95 > 200ms -> apply adaptive batching reduction and/or shed non-critical requests.

Capacity runbook checklist (quarterly):
1. Validate telemetry and billing alignment (token-matched metrics vs billing).
2. Recompute model-specific GPU footprints using latest profiling matrix.
3. Update autoscaler policies with new target utilization and burst settings.
4. Run scale tests for new regions or instance types.
5. Publish capacity report to stakeholders and schedule required procurement.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization
- All reliability work must be tracked in the reliability-initiative backlog board with an SRE priority score.
- Initiative scoring (example): impact * frequency * detectability -> priority. Use numerical ranges and thresholds in the board template.
- Types of initiatives: long-tail tail-latency reduction, distributional testing for model variants, KV cache warmup, cross-region fallback plumbing, autoscaler improvements, alert noise reduction.

Investment targets:
- Minimum 10% of engineering capacity should be reserved for reliability and SLO-driven work across the organization (adjust per quarter).
- Each major product area must have at least one ongoing reliability initiative tied to an SLO improvement or cost-per-token reduction.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)
Timing and authorship:
- A postmortem is required for: any SEV2+ incident, any incident that consumes >50% of an error budget, or any outage >5 minutes impacting customers.
- Owner: oncall who led mitigation must draft within 48 hours; service owner must review within 7 days.

Postmortem contents (required sections):
- Title, incident ID, severity, start/end timestamps, detection method, impact summary (customers affected, estimated revenue/usage impact), timeline of actions, root cause analysis (RCA), contributing factors, mitigation steps taken during incident, follow-up action items with owners and due dates, evidence attachments (logs, graphs), and 'what went well'.

Blamelessness and review process:
- Reviews are blameless and focused on systemic fixes. The postmortem will be reviewed in the next SRE incident-review meeting; action items tracked until completion.
- If a postmortem is judged low quality, it will be returned for improvement and the owner will be notified.

5) Operational Tooling and Observability Requirements
Mandatory dashboards and alerts per service:
- Dashboards: SLO dashboard (availability, latency p50/p95/p99, error budget burn), capacity dashboard (cluster utilization, GPU/CPU per-pool, queue depths), and recent deploys/rollout status.
- Alerts (examples):
  - svc_avail_slo_burn_high (trigger: burn_rate > 5x for 30m) -> pages SRE oncall
  - queue_depth_p95_high (trigger: p95 > 500ms sustained 10m) -> pages infra oncall
  - cluster_util_critical (trigger: util > 75% for 15m) -> pages capacity owners
- Instrumentation: all services must expose request-level metadata (route, model, customer_tier, token_count) to the telemetry pipeline with sampling rules for high-bulk customers.

Tooling standards and integrations:
- Primary metrics storage: Prometheus (short window) + Cortex/Thanos for long-term aggregation.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry with standard spans for request ingress, routing decision, runtime execution, and model payload read.
- Incident tooling: PagerDuty for paging, Statuspage for external communications, and a standardized incident Slack channel naming convention (#incident-<id>).

6) Runbooks and Oncall Playbooks
Runbook template (each runbook must include):
- Title / Service
- Owner and oncall rotation
- Symptoms and severity mapping
- Quick mitigation steps (ordered)
- Full diagnostic commands and queries
- Rollback and rollout guidance
- Post-incident actions and links to postmortem template

Example quick-mitigation (inference-router high tail latency):
1. Confirm: run prometheus query request_latency_seconds{job="inference-router"} and check p95/p99
2. Check recent deploys: /workspace/deployments latest by timestamp
3. If queue depth high, enable admission-control: curl -XPOST https://runtime-admin.local/disable-noncritical
4. Scale routing pool: kubectl scale deployment inference-router --replicas=XX -n prod
5. If root cause is a hot-model: route traffic to last-known-good model variant: POST /routing/override {"model":"<model-id>-stable"}

Diagnostic commands (examples):
- kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=inference-router -o wide
- jq '.events' /var/log/infra/events.log | tail -n 200
- curl -sS "${PROM_QUERY_URL}?query=rate(requests_total{job=\"inference-router\"}[5m])" | jq

Runbook escalation matrix:
- Page oncall (first responder) -> SRE lead after 30 minutes if unresolved -> Eng manager -> CTO for P1 incidents > 60m or high revenue impact.

7) Templates and Artifacts
- Postmortem template: link to /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template (use as required).
- Runbook template: link to /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-template.
- Capacity report template: link to /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-report-template.

8) Governance and Compliance
- Quarterly audits: ensure each production service has published SLO metadata and runbooks; eng-sre will run an audit and report missing artifacts to team leads.
- Confidentiality: internal by default; if runbook contains customer-sensitive remediation steps, mark confidentiality=restricted and follow security-and-compliance guidance for redaction.

9) Ownership and Contacts
- SRE lead: Ari Chen (primary contact for SLO policy)
- Capacity wg lead: Priya Nair
- Incident review chair: Daniel Park
- PagerDuty escalation policy IDs are maintained in eng-sre/team-wiki.

10) Appendix: Example SLO Calculation
- If service receives 100M successful requests in 28d, availability SLO 99.95% allows up to 50k failed requests over the window.
- Burn rate metric = failed_requests / allowed_failures_per_window. A burn_rate > 1 means the error budget is exhausted.

Revision history:
- 2026-03-04: initial draft (Ari Chen)
- 2026-09-12: updated capacity thresholds and autoscaler guidance (Priya Nair)
- 2027-04-22: clarified SLO change process and added tiers to error budget actions (Daniel Park)
- 2027-11-02: formalized runbook templates and added governance audit cadence (Ari Chen)

If you have questions or need a walkthrough, contact the SRE lead or open a ticket in the eng-sre backlog.
